arms.desc: Documented illicit small-arms and weapons trafficking corridors.
arms.label: Arms trafficking
arms.legend: Each arc is a documented illicit arms-flow corridor; thickness ≈ relative prominence.
arms.note: Direction-indicative corridors — arcs show documented flow directions, not measured volumes; illicit arms flows are diffuse and no comparable per-corridor counts exist, so every arc except USA→MEX stays qualitative. Scale anchors: ~1 billion firearms worldwide (Small Arms Survey 2017); ~70% of Mexico-recovered, traced guns are US-sourced and Canada is the #2 foreign recovery country for US-sourced crime guns (GAO/ATF); ~$7.2B of US equipment was left in Afghanistan in 2021, and the dominant Afghan flow now runs outward to the region. State-to-state major-weapon transfers are measured in SIPRI's TIV — a volume index, NOT dollars and NOT gun counts (global context: USA = 43% of all arms exports, 2024) — which is never mixed with the firearms figures here; most drawn arcs are illicit small arms, invisible to SIPRI.

sources.label: SIPRI — Trends in International Arms Transfers 2024
US GAO-21-322 — firearms trafficking to Mexico
Small Arms Survey — global firearms holdings

braindrain.desc: Emigration of doctors and nurses from their training country to wealthier destinations — a major strain on health systems in origin countries.
braindrain.label: Medical brain drain
braindrain.legend: Each arc is a major health-worker migration corridor; dots flow from the origin (training) country toward the destination.
braindrain.note: Labeled corridors carry measured stocks — UK nurse counts from the NMC register (Mar 2024), US counts by country of birth (ACS); unlabeled corridors are relative weights (OECD-DIOC 2010 rates), not head-counts.

sources.label: UK NMC — nursing & midwifery register data
American Immigration Council — immigrant healthcare workers
WHO — Health Workforce Support & Safeguards List 2023

cables.desc: Backbone submarine fibre-optic cables — the physical internet between continents.

edges.amt: 90% of Europe–Asia capacity · Red Sea crossing · 2023

cables.label: Submarine cables
cables.legend: Each arc is a major intercontinental submarine cable route carrying internet traffic.
cables.note: Routes are illustrative corridors from TeleGeography's cable map; capacity figures where shown are the design capacity of a single named flagship cable (Dunant, MAREA, 2Africa), not whole-corridor totals. Submarine cables carry >99% of intercontinental data traffic, and ~90% of Europe–Asia capacity funnels through Egypt's Red Sea crossing (~14–16 systems land there). Trans-Pacific corridors are weight-only — no per-cable figures compiled yet.

sources.label: Google Cloud — Dunant subsea cable (250 Tbps)

counterfeit.desc: Where seized counterfeit and pirated goods are documented coming from, plus known transit hubs and routes toward major consumer markets.
counterfeit.label: Counterfeit goods trade
counterfeit.legend: Arcs sized by % share of seizures where a real figure exists (China/Türkiye/UAE/Hong Kong → EU). Muted grey arcs are corridors or transit hubs backed only by a combined/group figure or no published split at all — hover for exactly what's known.
counterfeit.note: Global counterfeit trade is estimated at $467B, 2.3% of world trade (OECD/EUIPO 2025 report, 2021 data) — built from customs seizure data, an enforcement proxy rather than a direct measure, so results are biased by which countries enforce hardest and inspect what. Provenance is the last shipping/customs point recorded, not necessarily where goods were made — Hong Kong's figures are largely transshipped Chinese production. Data vintages differ by corridor since each comes from a different report: EU seizures 2024, US CBP FY2024, transit-hub routes ~2017. Two sectors have especially concentrated, differently-dated origin data not shown as arcs here: pharmaceuticals (India ~53%, China ~30% of seized value, 2014-16) and perfume/cosmetics (China ~78%, 2017-19).

sources.label: OECD/EUIPO — Mapping Global Trade in Fakes 2025
U.S. CBP — IPR Seizure Statistics FY2024

counterfeit.unit: % share of seizures or US$ seized (MSRP) where published; muted grey = no published % split

currents.desc: The great ocean surface currents that move heat around the planet — warm currents (red) carry tropical heat poleward; cold currents (blue) return.
currents.label: Ocean currents
currents.legend: Flowing lines trace major ocean currents. Red = warm current, blue = cold. Dots show the direction of flow.
currents.note: Schematic paths, not exact streamlines. Transports in Sverdrups (Sv) at the cited measurement section — western-boundary currents (Gulf Stream, Kuroshio, Agulhas) grow far larger downstream.

sources.label: Meinen, Baringer & Garcia 2010 — Florida Current transport (Deep-Sea Res. I)
Donohue et al. 2016 — Total ACC transport at Drake Passage (GRL)

debt.desc: Government-to-government lending: who owes whom. The teal end of each line is the creditor; the orange end is the debtor. Dots travel creditor → debtor.
debt.label: Bilateral debt (creditor → debtor)
debt.legend: Each line is a major bilateral lending relationship. Teal end = creditor (lender); orange end = debtor (borrower). Dots move from creditor toward debtor.
debt.note: Approximate bilateral debt-stock figures on two different bases: World Bank International Debt Statistics (public and publicly guaranteed debt, debtor-reported) and AidData (broader, including SOEs and swap lines — systematically larger, since roughly 70% of Chinese lending is non-sovereign). China → Argentina is mostly a PBOC central-bank currency swap, not project loans. Bilateral (government-to-government) debt is only part of total external debt — much is owed to bondholders and multilaterals (IMF/World Bank).

sources.label: AidData — Global Chinese Development Finance v3.0

debt.unit: US$ billions of bilateral debt stock (approx)

debtin.desc: Follow the money IN — each arc is debt a government owes; dots travel from lender toward borrower. Countries are shaded orange by how much they owe.
debtin.label: Debt — money owed
debtin.legend: Orange arcs = money owed, arriving at borrowers (dots move lender to borrower). Country shade = total owed (pale = little owed, deep red = heavily indebted; grey = no data). Click a country to isolate just where ITS debt comes from.
debtin.note: Same bilateral-debt data as 'money lent out', from the borrower's side. Approximate — World Bank IDS / AidData.
debtin.unit: US$ billions of bilateral debt owed

debtout.desc: Follow the money OUT — each arc is a loan a government has made; dots travel from lender toward borrower. Countries are shaded teal by how much they lend.
debtout.label: Debt — money lent out
debtout.legend: Teal arcs = money flowing OUT from lenders (dots move lender to borrower). Country shade = total lent (brighter = bigger lender). Click a country to isolate just the money IT lends out.
debtout.note: Same bilateral-debt data as 'money owed', from the lender's side. Approximate — World Bank IDS / AidData; Chinese lending dominates.

drugs.desc: Principal international drug-trafficking corridors, color-coded by substance.
drugs.label: Drug routes
drugs.legend: Each arc is a documented international trafficking corridor. Color = substance; thickness ≈ relative corridor prominence.
drugs.note: Afghan opium production collapsed −95% to 333 t in 2023 after the Taliban ban; global cocaine production stands at 3,708 t. Routes are directional — UNODC publishes no bilateral corridor tonnages, so widths are indicative, not measured.

dust.desc: Each year the wind lifts hundreds of millions of tonnes of Saharan dust across the Atlantic — fertilising the Amazon and feeding Caribbean skies.
dust.label: Saharan dust
dust.legend: Dust plumes carried west on the trade winds from the Sahara toward the Amazon and Caribbean.
dust.note: Schematic plume paths; tonnages are the peer-reviewed CALIPSO satellite lidar record (Yu et al. 2015, 2007–2013), not the older MODIS 240-Tg or NASA '40 million tons' popular figures. The winter–spring plume feeds the Amazon; the summer plume peaks in the Caribbean (Jun–Aug).

sources.label: Yu et al. 2015 — Trans-Atlantic dust transport (Remote Sensing of Environment)
Yu et al. 2015 — Fertilizing role of African dust in the Amazon (GRL)
Kok et al. 2021 — Global dust cycle (Atmos. Chem. Phys.)

flights.desc: Some of the world's busiest international passenger air corridors — the great-circle paths jets actually fly.
flights.label: Flight corridors
flights.legend: Each arc is a heavily-trafficked international flight corridor.
flights.note: Busiest international corridors ranked by OAG scheduled seats/yr — seat capacity, not passengers boarded. Labeled arcs carry 2024 OAG seat counts; the rest are real corridors whose exact figures sit behind OAG's paid data.

sources.label: OAG — Hong Kong–Taipei world's busiest international route 2024

flyways.desc: The great aerial highways billions of migratory birds follow between northern breeding grounds and southern wintering grounds each year.
flyways.label: Bird migration flyways
flyways.legend: Each ribbon is a major flyway; dots show the southbound direction of autumn migration.
flyways.note: The world's principal flyways; counts mix one-time censuses (stock) and birds/yr using a key site (flow), labelled per ribbon. Atlantic/Mississippi and Med/Black Sea totals are not established. Schematic.

sources.label: Wadden Sea Flyway Initiative — East Atlantic Flyway census 2023
CMS — Central Asian Flyway Action Plan

food.desc: The world's breadbasket flows - wheat, maize, soy and rice from the great exporters to import-dependent regions.
food.label: Food & grain
food.legend: Each arc is a major food/grain export route; dots flow from exporter toward importer.
food.note: Largest bilateral cereal & oilseed corridors, tonnes/yr, latest marketing year (USDA / FAO); marketing years differ by commodity. Russia has published no customs data since March 2022, so Russian splits are analyst port line-up estimates. US→China soybeans collapsed to near zero for ~6 months in 2025 on tariffs — 26.8 Mt is the last normal year. Corridors without a figure are relative weights only.

sources.label: USDA FAS — GAIN reports, GATS, PSD

migration.desc: Largest country-to-country migration corridors — number of people born in the origin country now living in the destination.

edges.dn: Displacement, incl. others in need of protection (UNHCR)
Displacement, incl. others in need of protection (UNHCR)

migration.label: Migration corridors
migration.legend: Each arc is a migration corridor with 1 million+ people (foreign-born stock, mid-2024). Thickness = millions of people and scales with zoom. Orange = majority displaced.
migration.note: All corridors with at least 1 million people, per UN DESA International Migrant Stock 2024 (POP/DB/MIG/Stock/Rev.2024). Stock = accumulated foreign-born population, not annual movement. Corridors that are majority refugees or people in refugee-like situations (per UNHCR) are shown in orange. Census timing and undercounting mean all figures are estimates.

minerals.desc: The raw materials of industry: iron ore, copper, bauxite, nickel, cobalt and lithium flowing mostly toward China's smelters and battery plants, plus the finished steel, refined gold and rare-earth magnets flowing back out.
minerals.label: Minerals & metals
minerals.legend: Each arc is a real, sourced mineral/metal corridor (2024–26, mixed vintages — see tooltip per arc). Orange = a brand-new corridor (Guinea's Simandou iron ore, first shipped Dec 2025). Grey = a transit leg with no independent volume figure (DRC cobalt via South Africa). Pink = China's rare-earth exports, sized for visibility rather than true tonnage since the real story there is leverage, not bulk. Gold = Switzerland's refined-gold hub exports.
minerals.note: Real, dated corridors from UN Comtrade, China's General Administration of Customs (via named market-data services: GACC/SunSirs, GACC/GMK Center, GACC/Fastmarkets, GACC/SMM), USGS, Australia's DISR Resources & Energy Quarterly, IEA Critical Minerals, and Swiss Federal Customs. A few figures are explicitly forecasts or partial-year: Guinea's Simandou volumes are 2027 targets for a corridor that only opened in Dec 2025; Brazil's 427 Mt is a 2027 global-supply forecast, not a China-specific figure; the UK gold figure is a single month (March 2026), not annualized. China's rare-earth magnet exports are shown at deliberately modest arc weight despite outsized strategic importance (58,000 t in 2024, ~94% of world sintered permanent magnets, and the subject of escalating 2025–26 export controls) — the story there is leverage, not physical volume. Two corridors (Switzerland→China, Switzerland→India) are real destinations per Swiss customs but this brief doesn't give a bilateral figure for either.
minerals.unit: mixed (US$ and tonnes per corridor — see tooltip; commodity trade isn’t one consistent unit)

oil.desc: Where the world's oil and gas move: from the big exporters (Gulf, Russia, the Americas, West Africa) to the big consumers (China, India, Europe, Japan).
oil.label: Oil & gas
oil.legend: Each arc is a major oil/gas export route; dots flow from exporter toward importer.
oil.note: Major crude-oil and LNG corridors, latest year (2024-25), from importer customs / EIA / national ministries. Crude in Mb/d or kb/d, LNG in Mt - not one scale, so arc widths stay indicative. Sanctioned Iran/Venezuela flows to China show ~0 in official customs (tanker-tracker estimates only), so no figure is shown. Routes thread strategic chokepoints - Hormuz, Malacca, Suez.

sources.label: US EIA - crude imports/exports by country
India DGCI&S; Japan METI; Korea KNOC; UK DUKES; Spain CORES

oil.unit: major crude oil & LNG trade routes

refugees.desc: Where the world's refugees have fled — forced displacement from conflict and crisis to neighbouring host countries.
refugees.label: Refugee flows
refugees.legend: Each arc is a major refugee corridor; dots flow from origin toward the host country.
refugees.note: Major corridors from UNHCR Global Trends; rankings and magnitudes are end-2024 vintage. By end-2025 Venezuela (6.5M) leads, ahead of Ukraine (5.2M) and Syria (4.9M) — the Venezuela figure includes 'others in need of international protection', not only Convention refugees. Most refugees are hosted in neighbouring countries; figures are relative.

sources.label: UNHCR — Global Trends / Refugee Data Finder (end-2025)

remittances.desc: Money sent home by migrant workers — largest country-to-country remittance corridors. Arrow points to the receiving country.
remittances.label: Remittance corridors
remittances.legend: Each arc is a major remittance corridor; thickness ≈ annual US$ sent. Arrow / dots point to the receiving country.
remittances.note: Top corridors from the World Bank–KNOMAD Bilateral Remittance Matrix, which is modeled (migrant stocks × incomes) rather than measured, is 2021 vintage, and is no longer updated (the KNOMAD portal went offline in 2024). USA→Mexico is the exception: $62.5B is measured by Banco de México for 2024 (96.6% of Mexico’s $64.7B total). USA→India is drawn at this map’s legacy weight (~$32B), but the 2021 matrix puts the US share nearer $6B and attributes most of India’s $129B inflow to the Gulf — treat that corridor’s size as unresolved. Figures are approximate and rounded; many smaller corridors are omitted.

sources.label: World Bank–KNOMAD Bilateral Remittance Matrix (via MPI)

shipping.desc: The arteries of seaborne trade — and the chokepoints they squeeze through: Malacca, Suez, Panama, Hormuz, Gibraltar, the Cape.

edges.amt: Suez ≈10% of world sea trade · 22% of containers
~3% of world sea trade · 9,944 transits FY24

shipping.label: Shipping lanes
shipping.legend: Each lane is a primary container-shipping route; the tight bends are the world's strategic chokepoints.
shipping.note: Schematic lanes tagged with each chokepoint's sourced figure. UNCTAD shares are % of world seaborne trade by volume (Malacca alone carries 23.7%), while the Hormuz figure is oil in Mb/d — different denominators. Post-2023 crises reshaped traffic: Red Sea diversions cut Suez container tonnage 82% (Feb 2024) and sent ships around the Cape (+12 days), and the drought-hit Panama Canal moved 423 Mt in FY2024, down 21% from FY2023 (511 Mt).

silkroad.desc: The network of routes that carried silk, spices, ideas, religions and plagues between China, Central Asia, Persia, the Arab world and Europe.

edges.amt: ~6,400 km · silk west, gold east · from 138 BCE

silkroad.label: Silk Road
silkroad.legend: Gold = the overland caravan routes; amber = the maritime spice route. Dots run west, as the silk did.
silkroad.note: Composite of the principal overland and maritime Silk Road corridors. Routes shifted over centuries; no reliable aggregate trade volume exists, so only datable facts (route length, dates, Pliny's contested sesterces) are cited.

sources.label: Valerie Hansen (Yale) — The Silk Road trade

silkroad.unit: overland + maritime trade routes (c. 130 BCE - 1450 CE)

students.desc: Where students cross borders to study — the flows of tertiary students from home countries to the big education destinations.
students.label: International students
students.legend: Each arc is a major international-student corridor; dots flow from origin toward the host country.
students.note: Enrollment stocks from each destination's own authority (IIE Open Doors, HESA, Australian Dept of Education, IRCC, JASSO, Campus France). Instruments differ — Canada counts study-permit holders — and 2024–25 policy caps cut Canada and UK inflows sharply.

sources.label: Australian Dept of Education; IRCC (Canada); JASSO (Japan); Campus France

trade.desc: Largest bilateral goods-trade relationships by annual value — the spine of the global economy.
trade.label: Trade flows (top exports)
trade.legend: Each arc is a major bilateral trade relationship; thickness ≈ annual goods value.
trade.note: US-corridor figures are US Census (2024, firm); other corridors are UN Comtrade via Trading Economics, with China-partner values on a China-reported “mirror” basis (mirror vs exporter-reported figures can differ 5–15%). DEU→USA, JPN→USA, ITA→DEU and NLD→DEU show 2025 (their latest full year), and NLD→DEU is inflated by the Rotterdam re-export effect. Some significant economies — Venezuela, Syria, Iraq, North Korea, Somalia — don't self-report to Comtrade at all and are only visible via partner mirrors, which is why they're absent from a ‘top bilateral flows’ view.

sources.label: US Census Bureau — Foreign Trade country balances

trade.unit: US$ hundreds of billions (annual goods, top bilateral flows)

trafficking.desc: Cross-border human-trafficking corridors — victims documented moving from origin countries to destinations for forced labour, sexual exploitation, or other exploitation. Only transregional corridors are drawn; most trafficking is in fact domestic.
trafficking.label: Human trafficking
trafficking.legend: Each arc is a documented cross-border corridor with 100+ victim case records (2002–2024). Thickness scales with case count (square-root scale, so smaller real corridors stay visible next to the largest). Color = dominant exploitation type: pink = forced labour, red = sexual exploitation, violet = other/mixed.
trafficking.note: Every corridor with at least 100 documented victim case records, 2002–2024, from the Counter Trafficking Data Collaborative's Global Synthetic Dataset v2026 (IOM, Polaris Project, A21, RecollectiV, OTSH). Counts are case records referred to these specific partner organizations, not a measure of true prevalence — they reflect where these partners operate and where cases get reported, which favors some corridors over others with real but less-documented trafficking. Individual case records are released as a differentially private synthetic dataset (statistically representative, not real people) specifically to protect victim identities — standard practice for data this sensitive, not a limitation unique to this layer. Corridor directions and widths are indicative of documented detection patterns, not measured trafficking magnitudes — detection data severely undercount true flows and are shaped by enforcement and reporting capacity. For global scale, UNODC's Global Report on Trafficking in Persons 2024 reports detected victims worldwide rose 25% in 2022 vs 2019, with victims of 162 nationalities detected in 128 destination countries.

sources.label: CTDC — Counter Trafficking Data Collaborative, Global Synthetic Dataset v2026
UNODC — Global Report on Trafficking in Persons 2024

trafficking.unit: documented victim case records (2002–2024, synthetic/differentially private)

voyages.desc: Four voyages that stitched the world together: Zheng He's treasure fleets, da Gama to India, Columbus to the Americas, and Magellan's circumnavigation.
voyages.label: Age of Exploration
voyages.legend: Each colored track is one expedition; dots follow the direction of the outward voyage.
voyages.note: Approximate tracks of Zheng He (1405-33), da Gama (1497-99), Columbus (1492), and the Magellan-Elcano circumnavigation (1519-22). Crew figures vary slightly across sources, and Zheng He's ~400 ft treasure-ship length is disputed (from a 1597 novel; scholars say 250-300 ft).

sources.label: Mariners' Museum — Zheng He / Columbus / Magellan

wildlife.desc: Illegal wildlife trade — ivory, rhino horn, pangolin scales and more, moved from source (poaching) countries through transit hubs to demand markets, overwhelmingly China and Vietnam.
wildlife.label: Wildlife trafficking
wildlife.legend: Each arc is a major wildlife-trafficking route; dots flow from source toward the demand market.
wildlife.note: Routes are direction-indicative, anchored to official poaching counts and seizure data — not total flow. Most China-specific corridor tonnages aren't published (destination attributed, not quantified). Vietnam, Malaysia, UAE and Singapore act as transit hubs; Nigeria's pangolin route has been disrupted since ~2022. Magnitudes are relative.

sources.label: South Africa DFFE / SANParks — rhino poaching

wood.desc: Where wood comes from and goes: boreal and tropical timber, lumber and pulp moving to the big manufacturing and construction markets.
wood.label: Timber & wood
wood.legend: Each arc is a major timber/wood-products trade route; dots flow from exporter toward importer.
wood.note: Largest bilateral timber, lumber and pulp corridors, 2024, raw UN Comtrade — m³ for logs and sawnwood, tonnes for pulp. Brazil→China and Chile→China are wood pulp, not logs. Russia stopped reporting to Comtrade after 2022, so Russian corridors use China-mirror import data. Several corridors are on the cusp of change from export bans (US→China logs, PNG→China, Gabon/Congo→China). Unlabelled arcs are relative weight only: Russia→Finland collapsed after 2022 sanctions (2021 baseline 4.6M m³ of logs), Myanmar→China's real teak trade moves informally overland outside customs data, and Russia→Japan has no sourced 2024 figure.
wood.unit: mixed (m³ for logs & sawnwood, tonnes for pulp — see tooltip)
